name: Embu
world_status: statement found in an open source
sweep_summary: Embu (embu1241) is not in the catalog. Two title-hit items: (1) Philippson 1991 (open PDF from DDL/CNRS, already fetched sources by the gwen1239 audit; copied into and read) — Embu is a '+' sample language with the author's own field notes, but the thesis has no Embu-specific prosodic statement or Annexe entry; the group-level claim (p. 451, p. 460, p. 485) is that Thagicu languages other than Kikuyu, 'semble-t-il', share the Kamba system: four Common-Bantu tone schemes plus a lexical opposition between (default) penultimate accent and exceptional final accent, the penultimate accent being demarcative and realised (in Kamba) as L-tone register, not length. (2) Torres Cacoullos & Travis 2014 is about English; Glottolog attached it to Embu by a computerized keyword misassignment ('patterning') — irrelevant. Best Embu-specific first-hand sources on file (earlier audit, re-checked) are Mwaniki 2014 pp. 30/33 ('tone, the only suprasegmental feature in Kiembu') and Nyaga 2014 p. 72 (emphatic penultimate lengthening); no source read gives a firm word-stress position for Embu. Lead for acquisition: Möhlig 1974 (Die Stellung der Bergdialekte im Osten des Mt. Kenya), Philippson's only Embu/Meru source, print-only (not an item here). web lookups, Crossref and Glottolog worked. updated.

earlier_scan.source_named: Philippson, Gérard. 1991. Tons et accent dans les langues bantu d'Afrique Orientale (comparative, covers Embu/Thagicu); not retrievable online (HAL/theses searches failed).

new_statements.quote: Hyman (1975) refers to stress, tone and duration as suprasegmentals of prominence. [...] The suprasegmental feature found in Kiembu is tone. Tone plays a very significant role in bringing out a number of contrasts such as in lexical differentiation, in tense and aspect constructs. [p. 30] [...] Mutahi (1977), states that Kiembu is a tonal language. [p. 31] [...] Kiembu has high (H) and low (L) tone. The tones are represented in lexical items across Kiembu lexicon on syllabic basis. [p. 32] [...] We have also looked at tone, the only suprasegmental feature in Kiembu. It has been noted that tone has a significant role in distinguishing the meaning of words. [p. 33]
new_statements.citation: Mwaniki, Daisy Gicugu. 2014. A synchronic survey of Kiembu dialects. MA research project, Department of Linguistics and Languages, University of Nairobi (supervisors J. A. N. Oduor & J. Mutiga). http://erepository.uonbi.ac.ke/handle/11295/76279
new_statements.locator: Ch. 2 'Kiembu phonemic inventory', sec. 2.5 Tone, pp. 30-32, and sec. 2.6 Summary, p. 33 (PDF pp. 43-46)
new_statements.reading: tone language with a stress statement
new_statements.rule_in_words: Kiembu is a two-tone (H/L) language with lexical and grammatical tone; the source names stress among the possible suprasegmentals and then states that tone is the only suprasegmental feature of Kiembu, i.e. no word stress is recognised. No stress position is given anywhere in the opened sources. A weaker secondary hint (Nyaga 2014: 72) is that vowels are lengthened in the penultimate syllable in emphatic speech, but that claim is borrowed from a Gikuyu thesis.
new_statements.exceptions: None; the tone section notes dialect differences in tone patterns (LH in Embu North/West vs LHLH in Embu East, sec. 3.2.4, pp. 39-40) but nothing about stress.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (lexical items in citation form, nouns and verbs); tone is discussed 'on syllabic basis'. Nyaga's penultimate lengthening remark concerns emphatic/reduplicated forms.
new_statements.identity_note: Mwaniki 2014 describes Kiembu proper (dialect areas Embu North/West vs Embu East, Kiruguru mentioned); Mbeere/Kimbeere (treated as a dialect of Embu in Wikipedia and in Mutahi 1977; Gatumu 2014 and Njuki 2012 are Kimbeere-specific) is not the variety of the quoted statement. Mutahi 1977 covers the whole Southern Mt. Kenya dialect continuum (Kikuyu, Embu, Mbeere). Glottolog's descriptive reference list for embu1241 is mostly keyword noise ('patterning'); only Biersteker 1984 and Saberwal 1968 actually concern Embu.

new_statements.quote: Cette apparition est due, d'une part, à la création de tons modulés lexicaux (selon des modalités que nous allons examiner) et, en kamba comme, semble-t-il, dans le reste des parlers du groupe, à une opposition entre accent sur la pénultième et accent sur la finale (se reporter au Chapitre cinq, 3.12.1). Je n'ai pas d'explication à proposer sur l'origine de cette opposition, autre que l'emprunt des thèmes accentués sur la finale.
new_statements.translation: This appearance [of new tone schemes] is due, on the one hand, to the creation of lexical contour tones (in ways we shall examine) and, in Kamba as, it seems, in the rest of the dialects of the group, to an opposition between accent on the penultimate and accent on the final syllable (see Chapter five, 3.12.1). I have no explanation to offer for the origin of this opposition other than the borrowing of finally-accented stems.
new_statements.citation: Philippson, Gérard. 1991. Tons et accent dans les langues bantu d'Afrique orientale: étude comparative typologique et diachronique. Thèse de doctorat d'État, Université Paris V. (Glottolog 38907)
new_statements.locator: p. 451 (ch. 6 §2.8.1, group XXII Thagicu); supporting p. 460 (typology a') and p. 485 (§3.5.3)
new_statements.reading: Group-level, not Embu-specific: Embu (E52) is a Thagicu language for which Philippson (who had his own Embu notes, p. 515) infers, hedged with 'semble-t-il', the Kamba pattern — a tonal language with a demarcative penultimate accent (realised in Kamba as register of L tones, pp. 368-369) contrasting with exceptional final accent on a minority of (mostly borrowed) stems; Kikuyu is explicitly excluded from this (p. 460, p. 485). The only first-hand Embu-specific statements on file remain Mwaniki 2014 pp. 30 and 33 ('The suprasegmental feature found in Kiembu is tone' / 'tone, the only suprasegmental feature in Kiembu'), which deny stress rather than locate it, and Nyaga 2014 p. 72 (penultimate vowel lengthening in emphatic speech, citing a Gikuyu thesis). Not a firm statement of word-stress position for Embu.

Thèse de doctorat d'État, Université Paris V (René Descartes), dir. J.M.C. Thomas. 542 pp. (Glottolog ref 38907; theses.fr NNT 1992PA05H011)
sources.quote: p. 451: "Mais, par ailleurs, de nouveaux schèmes sont apparus dans la plupart des langues.: 5 en kikuyu, 4 en kamba, etc. Cette apparition est due, d'une part, à la création de tons modulés lexicaux (selon des modalités que nous allons examiner) et, en kamba comme, semble-t-il, dans le reste des parlers du groupe, à une opposition entre accent sur la pénultième et accent sur la finale (se reporter au Chapitre cinq, 3.12.1)." — p. 485: "l'interaction entre l'accent (pénultième ou exceptionnellement final) et le système tonal, qui crée de nouvelles catégories prosodiques en chaga et dans les langues du groupe du Kenya Central." [Translation: new tone schemes arose ... in Kamba and, it seems, in the rest of the group's dialects, from an opposition between penultimate accent and final accent; the interaction between accent (penultimate, or exceptionally final) and the tone system creates new prosodic categories in Chaga and in the Central Kenya group languages.]
sources.locator: p. 73 (sample table: 'embu (E 52) +'); p. 451 (ch. 6 §2.8.1); p. 460 (ch. 6 §3.1 typology a'); p. 485 (ch. 6 §3.5.3); pp. 368-369 (ch. 5 §3.12.1.1, Kamba mechanism); p. 515 (own field notes list); p. 527 (bibliography 'EMBU, MERU: Möhlig 1974')
sources.note: Embu is a '+' (moderately documented) member of group XXII (Thagicu) in the sample and the author had his own field notes for it (p. 515), but the thesis contains NO Embu-specific prosodic statement and no Embu entry in the Annexe (only Kamba p. 513 and Kikuyu pp. 513-514). At group level: all Thagicu languages keep the four Common-Bantu tone schemes; in Kamba and 'semble-t-il, dans le reste des parlers du groupe' there is an opposition between penultimate accent and (exceptional, largely borrowed) final accent, analysed for Kamba (pp. 368-369) as a demarcative penultimate accent realised as…
